title: 3 Better Networking Questions
subtitle: The three questions to use at a career fair instead of the ones you could have Googled — and the one thing to do with the answers.
fromVideo: From the video: three questions that make networking useful
intro: Most students burn a career event asking what the company does and what a typical day looks like. Both are on the website. These three are not, because the answers only exist inside the person's head. Screenshot this page and open it in line.

entries.title: What part of your job took the longest to learn?
entries.lead: Ask this first. It is the one that opens people up.
items: You get the real skill, not the job description version of it.
It tells you what to start learning now, years before you would find out on your own.
People like answering it, because it is about their experience and not a test of the company.

entries.title: What do beginners in your field usually misunderstand?
entries.lead: This is the mistake question, asked so they do not have to call you a beginner.
items: You find out what everyone your age gets wrong, before you get it wrong.
It shows you are thinking about the work, not about getting hired today.
Listen for the word "actually" — that is where the useful part starts.

entries.title: What is AI changing in your work, and what skill would you learn first if you were my age?
entries.lead: Two halves, one question. Ask both together.
items: The first half tells you which parts of the job are moving.
The second half turns their whole career into one recommendation aimed at you.
You will get a different answer from every person. Collect them.

entries.title: Then do the part everyone skips
entries.lead: The conversation is not the value. What you do that night is.
items: Write down ONE tool, skill, or problem they mentioned. Just one, in your phone, before you walk away.
Research it that night while you still remember why it mattered.
Now the conversation gave you an actual next move instead of a business card.
entries.note: This is also the best possible follow-up message: "You mentioned X — I looked into it and tried Y."
